Milking Kimberley Psychiatric

By: Jana Marx | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Five years after it's openend, the Kimberley Mental Health Hospital, is in shambles, risking staff and patient safety.

Unique Selling Point:
Exclusive interviews with insider sources.
Undercover footage of the dire situation inside the hospital.
Interview with the Minister of Health TBC.

Summary:
In the early 2000s, the Northern Cape faced a severe shortage of psychiatric facilities, forcing patients to await placement in prisons due to insufficient hospital beds. Despite plans to build a modern mental health hospital in Kimberley, corruption scandals ensued, delaying construction and causing building costs to skyrocket.

The hospital finally opened its doors in 2019, but five years later, the rot of corruption is running deeper than ever, as the facility continues its struggle to provide even basic services and adequate mental health care.

When issues are raised, staff hears “there’s no money”, but Carte Blanche gold hold of a number of documents proving that inflated payments by the Department of Health in the province are eating away at the mental health budget meant for vulnerable patients. Nepotism among high-ranking officials have further worsened the situation.

The failure to fulfil promises to improve mental health services underscores the need for accountability and proper management to address the dire conditions affecting patients and staff in the Northern Cape.

Further information:
Shoot is split in two parts:

*Case studies, before they pull out (29 Feb)
*The rest of the interviewees (in March - dates TBC)

Press Release:


In the Northern Cape, government built what should’ve been a functional, modern, state-run mental healthcare facility. It was the long-awaited fulfilment of a promise to those in need of mental healthcare service in a province desperate for psychiatric facilities. But five years after it was finally opened, whistleblowers have come forward describing a facility that’s in urgent need of attention. And for once, a lack of funds isn’t the problem. Documents and images obtained by Carte Blanche show how the mismanagement of funds by the Northern Cape Department of Health and the hospital are eating away at the budget meant for vulnerable patients.

Script:


COMM 6519 l Milking Kimberley Psych Script

It was the early 2000s in the Northern Cape. Veronica Kasa, a court interpreter, received an alarming call from her 8-year-old son's school...

VERONICA: 02:46 There was a complaint from the teacher who said he was daydreaming. 03:00 So eventually they arranged an assessment with the Department of Education, where they had said that he must change schools.

With time, her son’s daydreaming became hallucinations… and he often turned violent.

Veronica supported him as much as she could, but as he got older, his needs grew and she realised he needed medical help.

At the time, there was only one small, understaffed psychiatric facility in Kimberley, servicing the vast Northern Cape.

So when the government began work on a large and modern psychiatric hospital, Veronica considered it a godsend.

The hospital would serve a large area with outpatient access, general psychiatric care, a forensic unit for accused people awaiting trial and a section for criminals who can’t be convicted due to mental health reasons.

VERONICA: 00:32:58:03 - 00:33:25:32: I was impressed. I was like, okay, so our kids are going to be assisted.

But her joy was short-lived. Construction limped along for 13 years – and a
290 million rand budget ballooned to about 2 billion rand.

This is the story of what’s become of that hospital.. and what it says about a province grappling with corruption and mismanagement. It’s about how people in the greatest need are paying the price.


ACT 1: A ‘MONUMENT OF CORRUPTION’

About a decade ago, Carte Blanche first reported on the Kimberley Mental Health Hospital.

UPS CB archive: Provincial politics severely affects the plight of psychiatric patients

It was among many projects in the tenure of then Public Works MEC John Block, who was jailed in 2016 for corruption and money-laundering in an unrelated case.

We reported how this grandiose construction was more than a decade late…

…and how, when it officially opened in 2019, it had been through four contractors and multiple lawsuits…costing seven times more than planned.

NORTHERN CAPE PREMIER DR ZAMANI SAUL UPSOUND: “this hospital also stands as a 6:27 monument of corruption”

Freelance journalist and author Charné Kemp has been reporting on the provincial Health Department and its hospitals for years.

ERIN: 00:01:43:41 - 00:02:07:29 So Do you think it's fair to say that it's been hounded by controversy both before the doors opened and once they actually did?
CHARNÉ: Yes, absolutely. After it opened, the DA went on the oversight visit and the then DA leader then said the hospital is filled with emptiness. And it was a very apt description because even though it looked very good,nothing happened there.

Oddly, Charne and her colleagues have been given little if any access to the facility.

CHARNÉ: 19:07 They're not really transparent about the services and the success stories that come out of that hospital. We haven’t heard of any.

But we have undercover evidence of what they appear to be hiding.

LINK: The Northern Cape Health Department has a terrible track record when it comes to Government expenditure. And their state-of-the-art mental health hospital in Kimberley has been a big hole since its build. But now, patients and staff are at risk…


ACT 2: WHISTLEBLOWERS

We were contacted by whistleblowers in January. Wanting to hide their identity, they described a facility so mismanaged that staff can no longer guarantee the care or safety of patients.

ERIN: You decided to speak out and to expose the hospital. Why?
ROGAN: I feel it is very, very wrong that people have to suffer and and patients have to stay in such terrible conditions. I couldn't stay quiet anymore. I had to speak out.
Erin: And what are the problems?
ROGAN: We’ve been without power since October last year.
The pharmacy had to relocate to the other hospital, because there’s no electricity. The medication has expired…

UPS UNDERCOVER VIDEO: “This is the closed pharmacy…”

Substations supplying power to the building haven’t been repaired after being vandalised…

…even a substation on the hospital grounds. It’s been out of order since October, with only two small and insufficient generators as back-up.

ROGAN: 10:24 The laundry room for our patients' dirty laundry is not operational.
09:36 I am at a point where I would buy washing powder for patients, so they can wash their clothes by hand.

We understand the lack of power means toilets can’t flush, as the sewage system is electrical.

VERONICA: I've been trying to use the toilets. They're very much uncomfortable. It’s a dark, it's a dirty toilet. That is not a place for a human being, especially one who has rights like that one of mine.

But the hospital's operational costs are well-budgeted for - the funds are just being mismanaged.

We obtained proof of numerous inflated payments, and it seems intermediaries added a hefty mark-up after acquiring the tenders.

Afraid for his job and life, we met another insider who echoed what the other whistleblower told us.
ERIN: 11:36 I want to show you something Carte Blanche got from a source. This is a golf cart. What do you know about it?
NOVEMBER: This is something I’ve seen in the hospital yard. I can confirm that.

The golf cart is used to shuttle people from the gate to the hospital entrance….
ERIN: What would you say if I told you the Department of Health paid around R500 000 for that six-seater?
NOVEMBER: That's crazy. That's very crazy. I can't believe it.
That’s the evidence we have. And it’s sitting at your hospital.
I can’t believe it…

If this cart was bought directly from the supplier, it would cost around 250 000 rand at most - not half a million…

ROGAN: 11:43 That hospital is boiling hot. Our patients eat cold food. 11:59 They bathe in cold water. 4:42 The hospital is in shambles. We call it the shanty.

UPS FROM UNDERCOVER: PATIENTS PRAYING: “Amen, guys. Enjoy your meal.”

We had more evidence.

ERIN: 11:39:26 A source also showed us this vehicle.
NOVEMBER: That’s a quad bike.
ERIN: Bingo, it’s a quad bike that’s been bought by the Department of Health for a mental health hospital in the Northern Cape. Please help me understand?
NOVEMBER: I saw a laundry aid worker riding it. I saw him riding the quad bike just for fun.
ERIN: With a trailer…?
NOVEMBER: Nothing. Just riding.

The quad was bought for R140,000. Its website lists it at R40,000.

While apparently able to afford a golf cart and a quad bike with a substantial markup, the hospital is failing at its primary task: patient care.

As a nurse, our whistleblower looks after the daily needs of patients.

ERIN: 31:28 So, we at Carte Blanche have proof of a linen order. Did you see any evidence of that order being delivered?
ROGAN: No, I have no knowledge of that, because if it was delivered it has to still be in the hospital today. Every single bed has one sheet - not even a blanket or a pillowcase.

However, our evidence shows an order placed in 2022 and another in 2023.

From the one order’s payment details, it’s unclear what the cost breakdown was - or even how many patients were purchased for. But working on the hospital’s current capacity of around 170 patients - and assuming they received either pyjamas OR linen – both would have cost R5000 per set. That’s right: R5000 for pyjamas or a set of blankets and sheets.

But there was worse to come.

ROGAN: 10:41 Our patients are not safe. There are snakes…Erin: Snakes? ROGAN: Snakes! Puff adders. It looks like a jungle around that hospital.

The fence that surrounds the high-security section that houses potentially violent state patients has been breached.

UPS FROM UNDERCOVER: The wire has been sectioned off where the patients broke it to escape.

ROGAN: 24:14 We are in danger. The doors are supposed to lock. But because there is no power, the doors stay open. So patients have access to us, the option to run away, access to hurt you. And remember, they know if they hurt us nothing would happen to them, because they're in a state hospital. But what about me? If a patient breaks out and stabs me - what about my children?

REFLECTIVE LINK: Under the circumstances, it’s amazing MORE staff haven’t quit. Some stay for the pay-check. Other refuse to abandon their duties. But what about the patients? They have nowhere to go?

To Charné, the allegations levelled against the hospital are inexcusable.
CHARNÉ: The Department of Health must take responsibility for that hospital and the other hospitals. They must.


ACT 3: TIME FOR ANSWERS

LINK: Amazingly, both the Head of Department and the CEO of the hospital agreed to speak to us. So we’re heading there now.

Albert Links has been CEO since 2019. He says security now patrols the facility day and night to prevent cable thieves from targeting the on site substation.

When we put the inflated payments of the quad bike, the golf cart and the missing linen to him, he told us his hands are tied - that the CEO’s job stops after requiring items from the Health Department.

ERIN: 17:01 So you're saying you can't do the things you want to do to fix this hospital?
CEO: In my space as a CEO, we do not administer supply chain. You eventually have to rely on your counterparts in the provincial administration. You do a requisition and you depend on turnaround from from them.

But, an expert in the sector told us a CEO is responsible for overseeing the hospital budget whether in charge of procurement or not, adding that a CEO, at the very least, should query or report suspicious payments.

Acting HOD for the Health Department, Mxolisi Mlatha, was appointed in December because the incumbent is facing fraud charges.

ERIN: 18:16 We understand from sources that there are a number of issues that are making it impossible for your nurses and your doctors here to fulfill the Hippocratic Oath. 19:03 That's your mandate.
Yes.
What do you say?
Look, we are dealing with the problems. But importantly, what what you must take into account. Here we are being impacted by what we call the social determinants of health. Things beyond us, things beyond our mandate.

He mentions the power issue as an example and how the Department apparently invested “extensively” in electricity provision. However, we learned from our insiders that the hospital would be cast into darkness for days on end because the generators ran out of fuel.

We also asked him about the inflated payments.

ERIN: Your own Premier Zamani Saul said at the opening of this hospital in 2019 that it was a monument of corruption. So I'm asking you pointedly, has it just changed shape over corruption, the kickbacks, the problems?
HOD: We have a process of getting to the bottom of of of of the allegations that are being made. We are determined to get to the bottom of, of, of of this and where there must be consequences, there will be consequences.

But the promises provide little solace to patients and staff bearing the brunt of government’s inaction and apparent indifference.

VERONICA: The government is failing me and other mothers out there.

And their state-of-the-art mental health hospital in Kimberley has been a big hole since its build. But now, patients and staff are at risk… ACT 2: WHISTLEBLOWERS We were contacted by whistleblowers in January. Wanting to hide their identity, they described a facility so mismanaged that staff can no longer guarantee the care or safety of patients. ERIN: You decided to speak out and to expose the hospital. Why? ROGAN: I feel it is very, very wrong that people have to suffer and and patients have to stay in such terrible conditions. I couldn't stay quiet anymore. I had to speak out. Erin: And what are the problems? ROGAN: We’ve been without power since October last year. The pharmacy had to relocate to the other hospital, because there’s no electricity. The medication has expired… UPS UNDERCOVER VIDEO: “This is the closed pharmacy…” Substations supplying power to the building haven’t been repaired after being vandalised… …even a substation on the hospital grounds. It’s been out of order since October, with only two small and insufficient generators as back-up. ROGAN: 10:24 The laundry room for our patients' dirty laundry is not operational. 09:36 I am at a point where I would buy washing powder for patients, so they can wash their clothes by hand. We understand the lack of power means toilets can’t flush, as the sewage system is electrical. VERONICA: I've been trying to use the toilets. They're very much uncomfortable. It’s a dark, it's a dirty toilet. That is not a place for a human being, especially one who has rights like that one of mine. But the hospital's operational costs are well-budgeted for - the funds are just being mismanaged. We obtained proof of numerous inflated payments, and it seems intermediaries added a hefty mark-up after acquiring the tenders. Afraid for his job and life, we met another insider who echoed what the other whistleblower told us. ERIN: 11:36 I want to show you something Carte Blanche got from a source. This is a golf cart. What do you know about it? NOVEMBER: This is something I’ve seen in the hospital yard. I can confirm that. The golf cart is used to shuttle people from the gate to the hospital entrance…. ERIN: What would you say if I told you the Department of Health paid around R500 000 for that six-seater? NOVEMBER: That's crazy. That's very crazy. I can't believe it. That’s the evidence we have. And it’s sitting at your hospital. I can’t believe it… If this cart was bought directly from the supplier, it would cost around 250 000 rand at most - not half a million… ROGAN: 11:43 That hospital is boiling hot. Our patients eat cold food. 11:59 They bathe in cold water. 4:42 The hospital is in shambles. We call it the shanty. UPS FROM UNDERCOVER: PATIENTS PRAYING: “Amen, guys. Enjoy your meal.” We had more evidence. ERIN: 11:39:26 A source also showed us this vehicle. NOVEMBER: That’s a quad bike. ERIN: Bingo, it’s a quad bike that’s been bought by the Department of Health for a mental health hospital in the Northern Cape. Please help me understand? NOVEMBER: I saw a laundry aid worker riding it. I saw him riding the quad bike just for fun. ERIN: With a trailer…? NOVEMBER: Nothing. Just riding. The quad was bought for R140,000. Its website lists it at R40,000. While apparently able to afford a golf cart and a quad bike with a substantial markup, the hospital is failing at its primary task: patient care. As a nurse, our whistleblower looks after the daily needs of patients. ERIN: 31:28 So, we at Carte Blanche have proof of a linen order. Did you see any evidence of that order being delivered? ROGAN: No, I have no knowledge of that, because if it was delivered it has to still be in the hospital today. Every single bed has one sheet - not even a blanket or a pillowcase. However, our evidence shows an order placed in 2022 and another in 2023. From the one order’s payment details, it’s unclear what the cost breakdown was - or even how many patients were purchased for. But working on the hospital’s current capacity of around 170 patients - and assuming they received either pyjamas OR linen – both would have cost R5000 per set. That’s right: R5000 for pyjamas or a set of blankets and sheets. But there was worse to come. ROGAN: 10:41 Our patients are not safe. There are snakes…Erin: Snakes? ROGAN: Snakes! Puff adders. It looks like a jungle around that hospital. The fence that surrounds the high-security section that houses potentially violent state patients has been breached. UPS FROM UNDERCOVER: The wire has been sectioned off where the patients broke it to escape. ROGAN: 24:14 We are in danger. The doors are supposed to lock. But because there is no power, the doors stay open. So patients have access to us, the option to run away, access to hurt you. And remember, they know if they hurt us nothing would happen to them, because they're in a state hospital. But what about me? If a patient breaks out and stabs me - what about my children? REFLECTIVE LINK: Under the circumstances, it’s amazing MORE staff haven’t quit. Some stay for the pay-check. Other refuse to abandon their duties. But what about the patients? They have nowhere to go? To Charné, the allegations levelled against the hospital are inexcusable. CHARNÉ: The Department of Health must take responsibility for that hospital and the other hospitals. They must. ACT 3: TIME FOR ANSWERS LINK: Amazingly, both the Head of Department and the CEO of the hospital agreed to speak to us. So we’re heading there now. Albert Links has been CEO since 2019. He says security now patrols the facility day and night to prevent cable thieves from targeting the on site substation. When we put the inflated payments of the quad bike, the golf cart and the missing linen to him, he told us his hands are tied - that the CEO’s job stops after requiring items from the Health Department. ERIN: 17:01 So you're saying you can't do the things you want to do to fix this hospital? CEO: In my space as a CEO, we do not administer supply chain. You eventually have to rely on your counterparts in the provincial administration. You do a requisition and you depend on turnaround from from them. But, an expert in the sector told us a CEO is responsible for overseeing the hospital budget whether in charge of procurement or not, adding that a CEO, at the very least, should query or report suspicious payments. Acting HOD for the Health Department, Mxolisi Mlatha, was appointed in December because the incumbent is facing fraud charges. ERIN: 18:16 We understand from sources that there are a number of issues that are making it impossible for your nurses and your doctors here to fulfill the Hippocratic Oath. 19:03 That's your mandate. Yes. What do you say? Look, we are dealing with the problems. But importantly, what what you must take into account. Here we are being impacted by what we call the social determinants of health. Things beyond us, things beyond our mandate. He mentions the power issue as an example and how the Department apparently invested “extensively” in electricity provision. However, we learned from our insiders that the hospital would be cast into darkness for days on end because the generators ran out of fuel. We also asked him about the inflated payments. ERIN: Your own Premier Zamani Saul said at the opening of this hospital in 2019 that it was a monument of corruption. So I'm asking you pointedly, has it just changed shape over corruption, the kickbacks, the problems? HOD: We have a process of getting to the bottom of of of of the allegations that are being made. We are determined to get to the bottom of, of, of of this and where there must be consequences, there will be consequences. But the promises provide little solace to patients and staff bearing the brunt of government’s inaction and apparent indifference. VERONICA: The government is failing me and other mothers out there.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Five years after it's openend, the Kimberley Mental Health Hospital, is in shambles, risking staff and patient safety.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Exclusive interviews with insider sources. Undercover footage of the dire situation inside the hospital. Interview with the Minister of Health TBC.
metadata.Summary: In the early 2000s, the Northern Cape faced a severe shortage of psychiatric facilities, forcing patients to await placement in prisons due to insufficient hospital beds. Despite plans to build a modern mental health hospital in Kimberley, corruption scandals ensued, delaying construction and causing building costs to skyrocket. The hospital finally opened its doors in 2019, but five years later, the rot of corruption is running deeper than ever, as the facility continues its struggle to provide even basic services and adequate mental health care. When issues are raised, staff hears “there’s no money”, but Carte Blanche gold hold of a number of documents proving that inflated payments by the Department of Health in the province are eating away at the mental health budget meant for vulnerable patients. Nepotism among high-ranking officials have further worsened the situation. The failure to fulfil promises to improve mental health services underscores the need for accountability and proper management to address the dire conditions affecting patients and staff in the Northern Cape.
